claims.claim: BHP links large-scale copper, iron ore and emerging potash supply to electrification/digital infrastructure, steel-intensive development and food security. Copper growth and Jansen diversify the portfolio, but geological endowment is converted into value only through permitting, safe execution, infrastructure and cost discipline.

Jansen shifts the potash thesis from project construction to ramp and market absorption; copper growth similarly shifts bottlenecks toward project delivery and capital efficiency rather than resource access alone.

risks.risk: Commodity substitution, recycling, demand destruction or new supply can reduce scarcity economics even when physical demand grows.
Permitting, construction, safety and cost overruns can shift resource advantage into capital impairment.

unknowns.unknown: Realized Jansen ramp economics and returns from the copper growth pipeline remain future execution questions.

claims.claim: FY26 record production and strong cash generation strengthen execution credibility, but results benefited from higher commodity prices and do not remove commodity-cycle dependence.

Jansen's prior Stage 1 cost increase from the original $5.7B estimate to $7.0-$7.4B is a concrete failure analog for megaproject cost/schedule risk; the FY26 contractor fatality at BMA is a present operational-safety weakness requiring continued control improvement.

risks.risk: High copper concentration in growth spending raises exposure to price assumptions, permitting and simultaneous-project execution.
Safety failures can impose human harm, operational interruption, regulatory response and loss of social license.
Megaproject cost escalation can erode expected returns despite strategically attractive end markets.

unknowns.unknown: Whether current cost discipline persists through the next heavy-capex phase and Jansen ramp is not yet demonstrated.
